problem: Learned end-to-end visual navigation policies are usually trained on data from a single robot, and each lab collects its own robot-specific dataset. The resulting policies do not transfer to new embodiments that differ in camera intrinsics or extrinsics, dynamics, speed or steering. So far there has been no evidence that one goal-conditioned policy can learn from heterogeneous multi-robot navigation data and control unseen robots.
motivation: Pooling data from many distinct robots could supply the scale that made pre-trained models so general in vision and NLP. Robotics data is fragmented across labs and platforms. The key observation is that wheeled robots, quadrupeds and even drones share the same abstract navigation objective (reach a goal, avoid collisions). A few simple design choices might therefore be enough to make cross-robot data sharing work.
key_idea: Train a single image-goal-conditioned navigation "omnipolicy" (GNM) on about 60 h of real-world trajectories from 6 different robots. It predicts in a speed-normalized waypoint action space and is conditioned on a temporal embodiment context of past frames, so it can be deployed zero-shot on new robots through a topological graph.
insight: The paper states that its contribution is empirical rather than algorithmic: cross-robot transfer mostly depends on three choices, all tested in the Table V ablation on an unseen LoCoBot. (1) Normalizing waypoints by each robot's top speed is decisive: normalized waypoints score 1.0/0.95 on Easy/Moderate, versus raw waypoints 0.42/0.26 and velocities 0.73/0.54. Raw waypoints actually do worse than velocities. (2) A temporal context of the last 5 frames lets the policy infer embodiment properties such as speed and turning. It matters most in hard environments: Hard SR is 0.36 with no context, 0.5 with static context and 0.7 with temporal context. (3) A conditioned architecture with an extra observation pathway (1.0/0.95) beats channel-stacking (0.52/0.72) and Siamese encoders (0.73/0.26). Adding more diverse data, even from seemingly unrelated off-road driving, generally helps. GNM-Mid and GNM-Large far exceed single-dataset and ImageNet-pretrained policies. The trend is not strictly monotonic: on LoCoBot outdoor, GNM-Small scores 1.0 versus 0.83 for Mid and Large.
method: Heterogeneous multi-robot dataset: aggregates 8 public or in-house datasets from 6 robots (TurtleBot2, Jackal, RC car, Spot, Warthog, ATV; speeds 0.2–10 m/s; office, hallway, suburban, sidewalk and off-road). Each dataset has forward-facing RGB paired with commanded actions and local odometry.

Shared normalized action space: the policy predicts τ=5 future relative waypoints p̃=(1/α)p(x,y) plus yaw ψ, scaled by a robot-specific factor α (the robot's top speed). It also predicts a normalized temporal distance-to-goal d̃. A robot-specific controller (e.g. PID, MPPI) unnormalizes and tracks the waypoints.

Embodiment context: the last k=5 consecutive observations are stacked with the current frame, so the network can implicitly infer the robot's viewpoint, speed and turning behavior without hand-designed robot descriptors.

Architecture: 85×64 RGB inputs. One MobileNetV2 encoder takes {o_t, C_t} and a separate MobileNetV2 encoder takes the goal image (context-conditioned design following RECON/CCRIG). The embeddings are concatenated and passed through FC layers to two heads: distance and waypoint sequence.

Training: following ViNG, positive image-goal pairs are sampled from the same trajectory and negatives from different trajectories. The distance head is trained on positives and negatives, the action head on positives only. Both use ℓ2 regression with Adam (lr 5e-4) and batch sizes of 400–1200 on multiple GPUs.

Deployment with topological graph (ViNG-style): graph nodes are prior observations (plus context) and edges come from predicted temporal distance. At each step the current observation and goal are localized in the graph, Dijkstra gives a subgoal sequence, and the policy is queried with the immediate subgoal to output waypoints.

setting.backbone: Two MobileNetV2 CNN encoders + fully-connected layers (trained from scratch with supervised learning)
setting.training_data: About 60 h of real-world navigation trajectories (Table I totals 70 h) from 6 robots and 8 datasets: GoStanford, RECON, CoryHall, Berkeley, SCAND (Spot and Jackal), Seattle, TartanDrive, NeBula. The evaluated variants use subsets: GNM-Small = first 2 datasets, GNM-Mid = first 4, GNM-Large = first 6. No simulation or web data.
setting.observation: monocular forward-facing RGB (85×64), current frame + 5 past frames as context, plus goal image
setting.action_space: 5 future relative waypoints (x, y, yaw) normalized by robot top speed, plus temporal distance; tracked by robot-specific low-level controller (velocities or motor commands)
setting.privileged: Topological graph of the environment built from previously collected robot observations (goal given as image); the robot's top speed α is known for action unnormalization.

numbers_note: This is a real-world-only paper with no standard simulator benchmark. All numbers are success rates that the paper defines as "mean progress made towards the goal", printed as fractions (0–1) and converted here to 0–100. The number of trials and environments per cell is not reported, except "20 indoor and outdoor environments" for Tables III/IV and 10 environments for the action-space ablation. There is a dataset-size inconsistency: the text says 60 h and 8 datasets, while Table I lists 9 rows totaling 70 h. The robustness results come from a small table inside Fig. 5.
results: A single GNM-Mid policy reaches mean success of 0.96 on LoCoBot, 0.99 on Tello, 0.93 on Vizbot and 0.94 on Jackal. It beats the best single-dataset policy on each robot (RECON: 0.62/0.79/0.26/0.68; GS: 0.51 on Vizbot) and controls a quadrotor never seen in training. On the unseen LoCoBot, GNM-Large reaches 1.0/1.0/0.83 (indoor easy / indoor moderate / outdoor), versus 0.35/0.35/0.57 for GoStanford+ImageNet. On the Jackal it reaches 1.0/1.0/0.88 (outdoor easy / outdoor hard / indoor), versus 0.72/0.52/0.31 for RECON+ImageNet. Under steering, viewpoint and physical degradations, GNM scores 0.89/0.81/1.0 versus 0.30/0.17/0.81 for a single-domain policy.
limitations: Assumes ground-robot-like navigation with a single forward-facing monocular RGB camera. Differences in capabilities (sensing, actuation beyond speed and steering, traversability) are not modeled explicitly, and the drone is restricted to a fixed-height horizontal plane.

Relies on a pre-built topological graph of prior observations and image goals, and needs each robot's top speed for unnormalizing actions. It cannot explore or follow semantic or language goals on its own.
The dataset is small (about 60 h). The real-world evaluation is small-scale, with success measured as mean progress and unreported trial counts, so results are hard to compare with other work.
